summary.title: Vim Commands: A Beginner Guide with Examples
summary.one_liner: You learn the basics of Vim: touch typing with home row keys, the NORMAL, INSERT, VISUAL and COMMAND-LINE modes, core motions, operators with text objects, and how to set options.
takeaways: Vim has distinct modes (NORMAL, INSERT, VISUAL, COMMAND-LINE) and you switch between them with keys like i, v, :, and ESC.
Keystrokes are composable: operators (d, c, y) combine with motions and text objects (iw, ip), e.g. ciw changes a word.
Navigate with h, j, k, l on the home row instead of arrow keys, and use motions like w, b, 0, $, f, t, gg, G.
Learn touch typing with the home row keys first, and keep a personal cheatsheet while practising.
Use :help, vimtutor, and the book Practical Vim to go deeper.
summary.summary: The article is a beginner introduction to Vim written by a developer who argues that learning Vim basics is useful even if you do not adopt it as your main editor. It starts with home row touch typing, then recommends installing Neovim and configuring vimrc, with example settings that disable arrow keys and set the system clipboard. The bulk walks through the modes, the command-line commands, search, undo/redo, insert variants, motions, the operator and text-object "language", and the set command for options. It ends with a summary and pointers to a second article, vimtutor, and Practical Vim.
